title: Checkpoint: Money and Government
objective: After this level you can explain how governments raise and spend money.
summary: Every budget ends with an audit. Independent auditors, backed by the 1977 Lima Declaration, check public money. Chapter 8: raise, plan, spend, check.

cards.headline: Every budget ends the same way: someone checks the receipts.
cards.body: Level 71's cycle had a fourth stage, audit, where the actual spending is checked. This chapter followed the money from taxes to pensions, bridges and tanks. This level follows the people who follow the money.

cards.headline: Auditors who answer to no minister
cards.body: Countries' top auditors are called supreme audit institutions. In 1977 they adopted the Lima Declaration, known as the Magna Carta of government auditing, and its chief aim is independent auditing. Level 76's European Court of Auditors shows the job: it asked not only 'was the money spent?' but 'did it deliver?', and found PPPs running up to 52 months late.

cards.headline: Follow one euro
cards.body: Try it with a single euro of tax. It arrives on the collecting side of Level 71's budget. The biggest share of spending goes on social protection, so it may well end up in someone's pension. If the government spent more than it collected, some of what it spent was borrowed. And after the year ends, an auditor checks that the money went where the budget said.

questions.prompt: What is the chief aim of the 1977 Lima Declaration on government auditing?

options.label: Lower taxes in every country
options.rationale: It's about auditing, not tax rates.

options.label: A single world currency
options.rationale: It has nothing to do with currencies.

options.label: Balanced budgets by law
options.rationale: It calls for independent auditing, not a budget rule.

questions.explanation: Known as the Magna Carta of government auditing, the Lima Declaration's chief aim is independent government auditing.

questions.prompt: The European Court of Auditors asked whether PPP money delivered results, not just whether it was spent. What does that show about auditing?

options.label: Auditors only count coins
options.rationale: It went further than counting: it asked whether the projects delivered.

options.label: Auditors decide next year's budget
options.rationale: Preparing budgets is the executive's job.

options.label: Auditors check results as well as receipts

questions.explanation: Audit is the budget cycle's last stage: checking what was actually spent and whether it worked, as the ECA did with PPPs.

questions.prompt: Money and Government recap: in Level 71's four-stage budget cycle, what comes right after the legislature approves the plan?

options.label: Auditors check the spending
options.rationale: Audit is the last stage, after the money is spent.

options.label: The plan goes back into the bag
options.rationale: The bag is just the word's history.

questions.explanation: The stages run prepare, approve, carry out, audit, so carrying out comes after approval.

questions.prompt: Money and Government recap: which three prongs did Hong Kong's ICAC use against corruption?

options.label: Fines, prisons and exile
options.rationale: Punishment is only one part of enforcement.

options.label: Audits, elections and referendums
options.rationale: Those aren't the ICAC's three prongs.

options.label: Taxes, tariffs and tolls
options.rationale: Those are ways to raise money.

questions.explanation: Since 1974 the ICAC has fought corruption through law enforcement, prevention and community education.

questions.prompt: Money and Government recap: what did Germany exempt from its debt brake in 2025?
questions.explanation: Germany's debt brake caps the structural deficit at 0.35% of GDP; since 2025, defence spending above 1% of GDP is exempt.
